job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Amira Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents in Valencia and commute to my master's in data science, which is mostly Python, statistics and a lot of group projects. In the evenings I help my younger brother Mateo with maths while my mother, who's a hospital nurse, comes home from a long shift. Last summer I did a three-month internship at the city transport agency, building a tool that predicts when buses will be late. I use an AI assistant now and then for debugging, but I always check what it gives me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but oversold, like most tech waves. At the agency my supervisor would roll her eyes and say we've heard this before. Online I'd keep quiet, because arguing about AI is a way to lose an afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel lucky. Companies still hire data people, my master's still counts, and my internship supervisor already said she'd write me a reference. I only worry that a quiet plateau could mean fewer new roles in public agencies, because budgets stay tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, apply to the transport agency again and two other public bodies, and keep using the assistant for boring bits like cleaning data. I'd keep paying a little each month into my savings, which my parents helped me start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm, though a bit flat. I wanted the world to be getting fairer with all this technology, and a plateau means it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said public budgets are tight. How does that affect your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agency can only hire when the city council approves a post, and last year they approved none. I'd apply anyway, but I'd also apply to a private logistics firm as a safety. I'd rather work for the public good, but I won't pretend I'd refuse a good private offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want more public money for tools that help ordinary people, like better bus timing. Right now the money goes where the profit is. A plateau keeps that exactly as it is.

say: I'd say AI is **useful but oversold**, like most tech waves.
I'd stay quiet online because arguing about it **wastes** an afternoon.
think: I feel **lucky** because companies still hire data people and my reference is lined up.
I worry public-agency **budgets** stay tight and posts stay frozen.
do: Finish the master's and apply again to the **transport agency** and two other public bodies.
Keep **saving** monthly and use the assistant only for data cleaning.
feel: I feel **calm**, though a little flat because nothing gets fairer.
S0.quote: I'd rather work for the public good, but I won't pretend I'd refuse a good private offer.
fieldNote: Amira is **secure** and knows it, with a reference and savings; her only worry is frozen public posts.
She is quietly idealistic and keeps a private-sector fallback without apology.
Her use of AI is practical and checked, never enthusiastic.

steps.text: Apply to the city transport agency and two other public bodies
Keep adding to my savings account every month
Use the AI assistant only for cleaning data

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to write rules, because the change is real and fast enough to hurt people. At the master's group chat I'd say learn it properly or get left with the leftovers. And I'd tell my brother Mateo that maths still matters, maybe more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my kind of work, writing code and cleaning data, is exactly what AI takes first. The junior analyst job I want is the entry rung, and firms may skip it. But someone has to check what these systems produce, and I think I'm good at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move from using the assistant now and then to using it every day, on purpose, so I understand its mistakes. I'd build a small project that audits a public dataset for errors, to show I can check machines. I'd also apply earlier and to more places, about 40 jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing on a train platform when the timetable has changed. I'm not panicking, I just need to read the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a manager who wanted to cut junior roles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep two juniors and give them different jobs: one to build, one to check. Checking becomes the product. A firm that has nobody who can question the output is one bad answer from a lawsuit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mother say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says nurses will be needed, and I tell her yes but the paperwork around her will change. She worries about me more than herself, which is typical. She's offered to cover my rent if I need a gap.

say: I'd say it's the moment to write **rules** because the change is fast enough to hurt people.
I'd tell classmates to learn it **properly** or get the leftovers.
think: Writing code and cleaning data is exactly what AI takes first, so the **entry rung** may vanish.
Someone must **check** what these systems produce, and I think I'm good at that.
do: Use the AI assistant **every day** on purpose to learn its mistakes.
Build a small project that **audits** a public dataset and apply to about 40 jobs.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, like reading a changed timetable on a train platform.
S1.quote: Checking becomes the product. A firm that has nobody who can question the output is one bad answer from a lawsuit.
fieldNote: Amira turns the threat into a **niche**: checking machines rather than competing with them.
Her family offers a rent cushion, which keeps her from panic.
She actively takes steps rather than waiting, consistent with her steady style.

steps.text: Build a project that audits errors in a public dataset
Send about 40 job applications by February
Use the AI assistant daily for coding and note my findings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, honestly, is too fast for anything fair. I'd say governments and unions need to be in the room now, and I'd join a data workers' group if there was one. To friends I'd say take any decent job you're offered rather than waiting for a perfect one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared. In 2028 I'd be 26 and the entry-level data and software roles would mostly be gone, which is precisely the door I'm walking through. The robots arriving around 2031 would only matter for physical jobs, so the thinking desk work is gone before I have a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the master's short if I got a good offer before the end, because a job in the door beats a certificate. I'd apply everywhere including hospital IT, which my mother's colleagues could introduce me to. I'd save everything and ask my parents about the rent gap they offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's scary and also a bit angry. I feel I was told to study hard and pick a safe field, and the field turned out to be the fastest-moving one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that sell this faster than anyone can adapt, and also governments that treated it as a tech story, not a jobs story. Nobody planned for a graduate class. I don't blame the machines, I blame the timetable people chose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mateo to learn how to fix things with his hands, or care for people, because those last longer. I'd say I'm not sure and that's okay. And I'd cook dinner, because it's easier than talking.

say: I'd say governments and unions must be **in the room now**.
I'd tell friends to take any **decent job** instead of waiting for a perfect one.
think: The entry-level data and software **roles** I'm aiming for would mostly be gone by 2028.
I feel the field I was told was **safe** turned out the fastest-moving.
do: Cut the master's short if a good **offer** arrives and apply everywhere, including hospital IT.
Save **everything** and talk to my parents about their rent offer.
feel: I feel **scared** and a bit angry about being told this field was safe.
S2.quote: I don't blame the machines, I blame the timetable people chose.
fieldNote: Amira's **blame** goes to timing and planning failures, not to the technology.
Her fallback is hospital IT through her mother's network, which is realistic.
Strong family backing keeps this at anxious, not alarmed.

steps.text: Apply to hospital IT teams through my mother's colleagues
Take a good offer before finishing the master's if one arrives
Save every spare euro and ask my parents about covering rent
Join a data workers' group and push for transition rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to see it and still short enough to scare me. I'd say publicly that we need retraining paid by the companies that benefit. To friends I'd say pick a specialty where being right matters more than being fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I get a window. By 2031 I'd have three years of experience, which makes me more useful than a new graduate. The thinking work goes then, so I'd have to be in a role that checks and decides rather than a role that produces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first good data job in a public body or hospital, and in year two I'd ask for the team that handles audits. I'd study for a certificate in data protection law in the evenings, because rules on AI create jobs for people who understand both. I'd keep a quarter of my pay in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a deadline I can see. Not calm, but I know what to do on Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why data protection law specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every company using these systems will have to explain them to a regulator. I'm good with detail, I like reading rules, and the people who can read both code and law are rare. It's the kind of niche a machine can't legally sign off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the niche gets crowded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I move again, maybe into policy work. I've learned that I'd rather plan a move twice than be surprised once. My mother says I overplan, which is a nurse's sentence about nearly everyone.

say: I'd say **companies** that benefit should pay for retraining.
I'd tell friends to pick a specialty where being **right** matters more than being fast.
think: I get a **window**: three years of experience by 2031 makes me more useful than a new graduate.
I need a role that **checks and decides**, not one that only produces.
do: Take the first good data job in a public body or **hospital**.
Study a data protection **certificate** in the evenings and save a quarter of my pay.
feel: I feel **tense** but clear: a deadline I can see and a Monday plan.
S3.quote: The people who can read both code and law are rare. It's the kind of niche a machine can't legally sign off.
fieldNote: Amira picks a **legal-technical niche** where human sign-off is required.
She plans second moves in advance, which fits her steady style.
Her mother's nurse habits shape her planning and humour.

steps.text: Take a first data job in a public body or hospital
Study a data protection law certificate in the evenings
Keep a quarter of every pay cheque in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is the version where good things can happen. I'd say we should use the decade to put rules in place and to share the gains, and I'd campaign for it in a party I trust. To friends I'd say don't treat it as a threat or a toy, treat it as a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay. By 2036 I'd be 34, maybe leading a small team, and I'd have lived through the change rather than before it. The robots around 2039 are a policy problem more than a personal one for my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a stable public sector role, build skills slowly and move to policy later. I might do a part-time doctorate in the evenings when I'm 28. And I'd help Mateo with his university choice, because a decade gives time for family plans too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels hopeful with a small edge. There is time, but time only helps if people use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you even in this slower world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That decision makers will wait. A decade can feel like forever and so nothing is done until year eight. I've seen it with climate plans in my own city, and I'd hate to watch it happen again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mother about her future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mother to retire when she wants, not when a machine decides. I'd say I'll help with the house. It's a promise I can keep with the salary I'd probably have.

say: I'd say we should use the decade to put **rules** in place and share the gains.
I'd tell friends to treat AI as a **tool**, not a threat or a toy.
think: By 2036 I'd be 34 and have lived through the change, not **before** it.
The robots for hands-on work are more of a **policy** problem than a personal one for my work.
do: Take a stable **public sector** role and build skills slowly.
Think about a part-time **doctorate** at 28 and help Mateo choose a university.
feel: I feel **hopeful** with a small edge, because time only helps if people use it.
S4.quote: I'd tell my mother to retire when she wants, not when a machine decides.
fieldNote: Amira is **hopeful** but fears institutional delay, citing her city's climate plans.
She links her own plan to family duties: Mateo's studies and her mother's retirement.
A steady planner who prefers gradual steps.

steps.text: Take a stable public sector data role and grow into policy
Help my brother Mateo choose a university course
Vote and campaign for rules on AI at work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one scares me most, because I'm at the start of my career and there's no time to build a base. What would help is paid transition schemes for graduates and a rule that companies must disclose when AI replaced a hire. My family's backing gives me room, but not everyone has that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd add that people my age are told to be flexible, but nobody tells the companies to be. I'd like to be asked more often what we'd build if we were allowed to.

headlineQuote: Nobody planned for a graduate class. I don't blame the machines, I blame the timetable people chose.
portrait: Amira is 24, living with her family in Valencia and finishing a **master's in data science** after a transport agency internship.
She uses AI now and then, and her answer to change is to **check** the machines rather than race them.
Her outlook is progressive and she wants rules, shared gains and **public-good** work.
In the two-year world she is scared but still has a plan, thanks to family backing.
With more time she picks a **niche** like data protection law and plans a second move in advance.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because she is at the start of her career with no time to build a base.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid transition** schemes for graduates and a rule that firms must disclose when AI replaced a hire.
